pieces.s: Youm7 said South Africa is entering a new political phase after an unprecedented fall for the ANC, punished for failures in water, electricity and infrastructure and now forced into coalition talks in major cities. Citing Reuters, it put the ANC on about 31%, the DA on 25% and MK on about 10%. It cited the Auditor-General’s finding that only 39 municipalities, 15%, had clean audits, with R14.73 billion lost on water and R21.63 billion on electricity.

pieces.s: A Japanese translation of Reuters’ report. The ANC stayed the largest party but fell to 30.76% from 45.59% in 2021, and many cities, Johannesburg included, have no majority party and face coalition talks. In Johannesburg the DA won about 35% against about 20% for the ANC, and the number of cities needing coalitions more than doubled. Ramaphosa urged parties to negotiate with humility.

stories.h: Abroad, Johannesburg is the story: a deal to shut out the DA
stories.dek: Johannesburg gets the most attention outside South Africa. Reuters and the FT reported that the ANC and its partners were close to a deal that would sideline the DA, which won the most votes in the city. The FT reported that Helen Zille had told allies her bid for mayor was over, and The Africa Report called Herman Mashaba the kingmaker in Gauteng.
brief: Reuters reported on 19 November that the ANC and its partners were near a deal that would sideline the DA in Johannesburg, though the DA topped the poll there
The FT had reported the ANC nearing a coalition deal in the city the day before
The FT then reported that Helen Zille, whom it calls South Africa’s “Iron Lady”, had told allies her mayoral bid was over
The Africa Report named Herman Mashaba the kingmaker in Gauteng
For foreign readers, the story is that the party with the most votes may not govern Africa’s richest city
sec: The angle abroad
Foreign outlets tell the Johannesburg story through the paradox at its centre: the DA won the most votes but may be shut out of power. Reuters puts that paradox in its headline.
What they leave out

Judging by their headlines, foreign outlets give less room than South African ones to the share-out of mayoral posts or the timing of council sittings. They focus on who ends up in charge and what that says about the ANC.

stories.h: What the city deals mean for the unity government
stories.dek: Foreign outlets keep asking whether the local fights will spill into the national unity government. Bloomberg reported that the DA would stay in the GNU for now. Semafor’s Sam Mkokeli called the metros an urban test for it, Justice Malala argued in Bloomberg Opinion that the coalition government has to succeed, and Bloomberg’s Next Africa podcast asked whether it could collapse.

sec: The angle abroad

Outside South Africa, the city talks matter mostly for what they mean for the national government formed in 2024. The question foreign outlets keep asking is whether a DA shut out of the metros will stay in the GNU, and what happens to investor confidence if it does not.
Why it matters to them
For investors and foreign governments, the GNU is the main sign of stability after the ANC lost its majority. That is why Bloomberg treats the DA’s decision to stay as news in itself.

stories.h: The rand slides as investors watch the talks
stories.dek: Financial outlets link the talks to the currency. Reuters reported the rand at a seven-month low on 17 November as traders tracked the coalition talks, and near a one-year low two days later. Bloomberg reported it testing R17 to the dollar with the focus on politics, and Michael Cohen wrote that the messy fallout had rattled investors.

sec: The angle abroad

This is the part of the story covered almost only by foreign and financial outlets. They read the coalition talks as political risk, and track the talk of the ANC turning away from the DA through the rand.
What to watch
Wire and markets reporters link moves in the currency to news from the talks. A signed deal in Gauteng, or any sign of strain in the GNU, is likely to show up in their market reports first.

stories.h: South Africa’s cities move to coalition rule
stories.dek: Straight after the results, Bloomberg and Reuters reported that the biggest cities would be run by coalitions, and AP described high-stakes talks after the ANC’s worst result. Two weeks on, Bloomberg’s S’thembile Cele wrote that post-election bartering was counting for more than votes, while the FT and the BBC reported the ANC fighting to keep control of key cities.

Bloomberg later wrote that post-election bartering was counting for more than votes
sec: The angle abroad

Foreign outlets explain coalition rule as something new for readers who know South Africa as a one-party story. Their pieces describe hung councils as a sign of a fragmenting vote rather than as a contest between named candidates.
The bargaining
By the third week, the framing had shifted from the ANC’s losses to the deal-making. Bloomberg’s S’thembile Cele wrote that bartering after the vote was mattering more than the vote itself.

stories.h: A turning point for Mandela’s party
stories.dek: Many foreign pieces treat the result as a turning point for the ANC. The New York Times’ John Eligon wrote that South Africa’s politics may never be the same again. The Economist welcomed voters giving up on the party, AP explained how it lost its way, and the FT reported on townships turning against it.

sec: The angle abroad
Most foreign pieces open with Nelson Mandela. They treat the result as the end of an era for a liberation movement that readers abroad still associate with 1994, more than as a municipal election.
Where they disagree
The tone varies. The Economist welcomes the decline as good for South Africa, while AP and the FT look at what drove voters away, including anger in the townships.
